{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-wi-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"be8cdf0713903e70e3156ce189ba20fc43e9790a69dec8f3c2f35cb07cbafd2c","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-wi-class-d:lineage:67","source_registry_sha256":"9dcfc0d0c3044debd01d4cb03103f48fb860797364a23b2cb56d36c868619a64","source_liveness_sha256":"4ca51030ff51b3372629ada1c05ad91f501dabccdcf7931dab678c717e7bb9b6"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sign confusables: look-alike shapes and colors, lane-use sign variants, route marker shapes and railroad crossing sign types","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: stop versus yield, yellow warning versus orange work-zone signs, green, brown and blue guide signs, roundabout lane-use variants, route marker shapes and railroad crossing sign types","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: stop versus yield, yellow warning versus orange work-zone signs, green, brown and blue guide signs, roundabout lane-use variants, route marker shapes and railroad crossing sign types
Confusable pairs and continuation facts for the signs chapter, where similar colors, shapes and lane-use layouts are easy to mix up; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec05-R01 | anchor: A01
An Intersection or Cross Road warning sign marks a spot ahead where two or more roads cross each other. [A01]
Why it matters: group warning signs; continuation; prereq right-of-way at intersections.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-R02 | anchor: A02
A Sharp Turn sign can point left or right and asks you to be ready to slow for the turn, unlike a Curved Road sign, which marks a gradual bend [A02] [A01].
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable sharp turn versus curved road.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-R03 | anchor: A02
A Curved Road sign warns that the road bends gradually right or left, and you slow only as much as needed to drive it safely. [A02]
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable curved road versus sharp turn.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-R04 | anchor: A01
A Merge sign shows a lane joining from the right or left, while a Lane Ends sign shows your own lane ending; in both cases you move over when it is safe [A01] [A02].
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable merge versus lane ends.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-R05 | anchor: A02
A Hill sign warns of a hill ahead, and you slow down if needed to stay safe. [A02]
Why it matters: group warning signs; continuation.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-R06 | anchor: A03
A No Turn sign points toward the direction you may not turn, while a No U-turn sign forbids turning around. [A03]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable no turn versus no U-turn.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-R07 | anchor: A03
Reduced Speed Ahead is a regulatory sign meaning you should slow down because a curb or slippery road might lie ahead [A03].
Why it matters: group sign families; confusable warning versus regulatory.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-R08 | anchor: A03
In the two-lane roundabout example, the left lane is only for turning left or making a U-turn, and the right lane is for going straight or turning right. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane-use signs; confusable left lane versus right lane; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-R09 | anchor: A04
In the three-lane roundabout example, the far-left lane turns left or goes straight, the middle lane goes straight, and the right lane turns right. [A04]
Why it matters: group lane-use signs; confusable three-lane versus two-lane layout; difficulty hard.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-R10 | anchor: A04
In the second two-lane roundabout lane-use sign example, the far-left lane is used only to turn left while the right lane is used to turn left or go straight [A04].
Why it matters: group lane-use signs; misconception the right lane never turns left.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-R11 | anchor: A04
A Stop sign is red with white letters and eight sides and requires a complete stop, while a Yield sign is a downward red and white triangle that requires giving the right-of-way to other vehicles. [A04]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable stop versus yield.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-R12 | anchor: A04
The orange Slow Moving Vehicle triangle marks a vehicle that may travel at 25 mph or less, while the yellow No Passing Zone pennant forbids passing. [A04]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; confusable triangle versus pennant.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-R13 | anchor: A05
Orange diamond or rectangular construction signs have black lettering and symbols that warn about construction, maintenance, or emergency workers on or near the road [A05].
Why it matters: group sign colors; confusable yellow versus orange.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-R14 | anchor: A05
A flagger's directions must be followed, while the Road Workers Ahead sign asks you to slow down or move over for workers ahead. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; confusable flagger versus road workers sign.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-R15 | anchor: A06
Green and brown guide signs both give directions to places, but the brown ones point to fun or scenic places such as parks. [A06]
Why it matters: group guide signs; confusable green versus brown.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-R16 | anchor: A06
Blue signs point to services such as a hospital or camping, while green and brown signs point to destinations [A06] [A07].
Why it matters: group guide signs; confusable blue service versus green destination.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-R17 | anchor: A07
Mile markers can be blue or green but are recognized by their tall, thin shape and the direction, route and mile number they carry. [A07]
Why it matters: group mile markers; confusable mile marker versus service sign.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-R18 | anchor: A08
A county road sign is a white rectangle with rounded edges and black letters. [A08]
Why it matters: group route markers; confusable county versus state.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-R19 | anchor: A08
A U.S. route sign looks like a police badge and is usually grey or white with black letters, unlike the red and blue interstate shield. [A08]
Why it matters: group route markers; confusable U.S. route versus interstate.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-R20 | anchor: A08
A state road sign is shaped like a milk jug with its spout at the bottom and is white with black letters. [A08]
Why it matters: group route markers; confusable state versus county.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-R21 | anchor: A09
A Tracks out-of-service sign means the tracks are no longer used, while an Exempt sign means only certain vehicles are excused from stopping before crossing. [A09]
Why it matters: group railroad signs; confusable out-of-service versus exempt.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R22 | anchor: A09
The round yellow railroad warning sign with an X tells you a crossing is there, while the white X-shaped crossbuck also lists how many tracks you will cross. [A09]
Why it matters: group railroad signs; confusable round warning sign versus crossbuck.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R23 | anchor: A10
When a crossing has two sets of tracks, wait until the train is far enough away that you can see the other tracks are clear. [A10]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; misconception go as soon as the train passes.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]
